idiom_name: state in Mutex<T>, non-locking methods on the guarded type, one locking entry method
implementation_notes: Rust makes the split structural: std::sync::Mutex owns the value it protects and only hands it out through a MutexGuard, so the natural realization is an inner state type whose methods take &mut self and never lock, plus a thin wrapper whose methods take &self, lock once and call the inner methods through the guard. The guard is the proof that the lock is held - without it there is no &mut access - so the classic *_impl naming convention becomes a type-level precondition, while locking twice on the same thread is a documented hazard: the second lock blocks and the standard library may panic. The std guard is not Send and must not be held across .await, so async components use tokio::sync::Mutex (or parking_lot for a faster, non-poisoning mutex); dedicated reentrant mutexes exist in the ecosystem but are the workaround the pattern avoids.
pitfalls: std::sync::Mutex is not reentrant: locking it twice on the same thread blocks, and lock is documented to possibly panic when the current thread already holds it; reentrant mutex crates reintroduce the workaround this pattern removes.
A multi-statement critical section built from chained temporaries silently drops the guard at the end of the statement, so the later statements run unprotected.
MutexGuard is not Send: a std guard held across .await does not compile for Send futures - use tokio::sync::Mutex and keep the non-locking helpers non-async.

Poisoning: an inner method that panics while the guard is held poisons the mutex and later lock().unwrap() calls panic too - decide deliberately between unwrap, poison().into_inner() and a non-poisoning mutex.
The inner methods must not take &self and lock internally, or the type-level precondition disappears and the wrapper locks twice.
